power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Introduction: Acellular scleral allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis is a bio-interventional surgery (BIOS) to lower intraocular pressure (IOP).
We report 2-year efficacy and safety outcomes when the procedure is performed in combination with phacoemulsification and as a standalone procedure in eyes with open-angle glaucoma.
Methods: Analysis of the multicenter CREST real-world evidence study of eyes undergoing allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis with AlloFlo™ Uveo (Iantrek, Inc., White Plains, NY; NCT05506423).
Eyes attending the Month-24 visit were analyzed: 176 eyes undergoing phacocombined surgery (Cohort 1) and 32 standalone eyes (Cohort 2).
Values recorded after secondary procedures censored.
Cohort 1 only was stratified by low, moderate, or high baseline IOP (≤ 15, 16-20, ≥ 21 mmHg).
Results: A total of 176 eyes in Cohort 1 and 32 in Cohort 2 were analyzed.

In Cohort 1, IOP decreased 3.1 mmHg at Month 24 from a baseline of 18.0 (-12.5%; p < 0.001), and medications decreased 0.5 from 1.5 (p < 0.001); medication-free eyes rose from 22.9% to 46.4% (p < 0.001).
text.formatted: In Cohort 1, IOP decreased 3.1 mmHg at Month 24 from a baseline of 18.0 (-12.5%; p < 0.001), and medications decreased 0.5 from 1.5 (p < 0.001); medication-free eyes rose from 22.9% to 46.4% (p < 0.001).

text.text: IOP changes in the low, moderate, and high baseline tiers were +0.9 (+7.8%), -3.0 (-16.3%), and -9.2 (-36.1%) mmHg; medication changes were -0.8, -0.6, and +0.1.
In Cohort 2, IOP decreased 6.4 mmHg from 20.0 (-27.1%; p < 0.001), and medications decreased 1.2 from 2.8 (p = 0.004); medication-free eyes rose from 4.3% to 30.4% (p = 0.031).
text.formatted: In Cohort 2, IOP decreased 6.4 mmHg from 20.0 (-27.1%; p < 0.001), and medications decreased 1.2 from 2.8 (p = 0.004); medication-free eyes rose from 4.3% to 30.4% (p = 0.031).

text.text: Secondary IOP-lowering procedures were performed in 5.1% of Cohort 1 eyes and 28.1% of Cohort 2.
Kaplan-Meier freedom from reoperation was 98.9% and 84.4%.
No eye developed clinically significant hypotony or choroidal effusion, and there were no allograft-related vision-threatening adverse events.
Conclusion: Allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis effectively lowered IOP and medication use through 24 months.

• When performed as a standalone procedure, pressure decreased 6.4 mmHg and 78 medications by 1.2, and medication-free eyes rose from 4.3% to 30.4%, reflecting 79 promising outcomes in refractory eyes.
80 • No eye developed clinical hypotony, choroidal effusion, or corneal decompensation, and 81 endothelial cell loss was confined to the phacoemulsification-combined cohort.
Freedom 82 from reoperation at 24 months was 98.9% with cataract surgery and 84.4% standalone.
Cataract and glaucoma frequently coexist.
Lens extraction alone lowers intraocular pressure (IOP) by approximately 2-4 mmHg in glaucomatous eyes, with greater reductions associated with higher preoperative IOP [1] [2] [3] [4] [5].
text.formatted: Lens extraction alone lowers intraocular pressure (IOP) by approximately 2-4 mmHg in glaucomatous eyes, with greater reductions associated with higher preoperative IOP <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref>.

text.text: Phacoemulsification combined with minimally invasive glaucoma surgery (MIGS) is routinely performed when additional IOP control or a reduction in medication burden is warranted.

The incremental efficacy of the most widely used trabecular and canalicular devices over phacoemulsification alone is modest: pivotal randomized trials demonstrated between-group differences of 1.6-2.3 mmHg in unmedicated diurnal IOP reduction at 24 months [6, 7].
text.formatted: The incremental efficacy of the most widely used trabecular and canalicular devices over phacoemulsification alone is modest: pivotal randomized trials demonstrated between-group differences of 1.6-2.3 mmHg in unmedicated diurnal IOP reduction at 24 months <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7]</ref>.

text.text: Canal interventions are mostly proximal to the collector channels and episcleral veins, and their pressure-lowering efficacy is therefore constrained by distal outflow resistance and episcleral venous pressure.

The uveoscleral pathway permits aqueous humor to traverse the ciliary interstitium into the supraciliary and suprachoroidal spaces, without the lower pressure limit imposed by episcleral venous pressure.
Surgical cyclodialysis accesses this pathway, but its outcomes have historically been unpredictable.
Cyclodialysis clefts are susceptible to spontaneous postoperative closure, which can cause IOP spikes and diminish the pressure-lowering effect.
Cleft reinforcement is therefore indicated to maintain patency and provide sustained IOP reduction.

Scleral allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis entails creation of a controlled ab-interno cyclodialysis cleft and placement of shaped segments of minimally modified homologous, non-resorbable human scleral allograft within the supraciliary space to maintain cleft patency [8].
text.formatted: Scleral allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis entails creation of a controlled ab-interno cyclodialysis cleft and placement of shaped segments of minimally modified homologous, non-resorbable human scleral allograft within the supraciliary space to maintain cleft patency <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref>.

text.text: Published studies have reported first-in-human results, 12-month multicenter outcomes, safety outcomes in a large clinical series, single-center 24-month outcomes, and 12-month outcomes following standalone surgery [8] [9] [10] [11] [12].
text.formatted: Published studies have reported first-in-human results, 12-month multicenter outcomes, safety outcomes in a large clinical series, single-center 24-month outcomes, and 12-month outcomes following standalone surgery <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref>.

text.text: However, multicenter safety and efficacy outcomes at 24 months have not yet been reported.

We report 24-month outcomes from two parallel cohorts of the CREST registry: phacoemulsification combined with allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis in phakic eyes (Cohort 1), and standalone allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis (Cohort 2).
The cohorts answer different clinical questions and differ in lens status, baseline IOP, and referral pattern, so they are characterized in parallel and not compared with each other.
Because IOP dependence on baseline pressure is a recurrent theme in MIGS reporting [5, 13], we examined it in the combined Cohort 1 as an exploratory analysis [14].
text.formatted: Because IOP dependence on baseline pressure is a recurrent theme in MIGS reporting <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref>, we examined it in the combined Cohort 1 as an exploratory analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref>.

text.text: Enrollment numbers in the standalone cohort did not support subgroup stratification in the standalone Cohort 2.

CREST (NCT05506423) is a prospective, multicenter, observational real-world evidence study that enrolls recipients of allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis using the AlloFlo Uveo™ system (Iantrek, Inc., White Plains, NY) at 17 sites in the United States and Central America.
The study includes broad real-world inclusion criteria (diagnosis of open-angle glaucoma and bioreinforced cyclodialysis was attempted) with no exclusion criteria.

Per-protocol, eyes are enrolled into one of two cohorts: Cohort 1 comprises eyes that underwent the study procedure concurrent with phacoemulsification in a single surgical session; Cohort 2 comprises eyes that underwent a standalone study procedure.
As a real-world study, there is no medication washout, and treating surgeons have postoperative discretion to medicate eyes according to need and clinical best practice.
Likewise, there are no postoperative medication or treatment policies in the CREST protocol.
Eyes in the present analysis were required to have had at least 24 months of post-surgical followup to allow for adequate long-term analysis of efficacy and safety.
The present analysis reports outcomes as of the most recent data cutoff (31 January 2026).
text.formatted: The present analysis reports outcomes as of the most recent data cutoff <ref type="bibr">(31 January 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The CREST study is conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki, under oversight of Advarra IRB (approval MOD02608603).
All participants gave written informed consent.
The ab-interno bio-interventional surgical (BIOS) technique has been previously described [8, 9].
text.formatted: The ab-interno bio-interventional surgical (BIOS) technique has been previously described <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">9]</ref>.

text.text: Briefly, under topical or intracameral anesthesia, a cyclodialysis cleft is created in the supraciliary space and then acellular scleral allograft bio-scaffolds are placed in the cleft.

The allograft spacer is composed of microtrephined scleral donor tissue (5 mm × 500 µm each), rather than a rigid polymer, and the procedure preserves the conjunctiva and does not result in a filtering bleb.
Allograft tissue is processed in a minimally modified standard and comes preloaded in a handheld delivery cannula.
The number of segments and quadrant were at the treating surgeon's discretion.
Postoperative medications and the decision to withhold or continue glaucoma medications followed each surgeon's best practice for the individual patient and eye.
IOP was measured by Goldmann applanation tonometry.
Baseline IOP was the medicated IOP at the preoperative visit on the patient's current regimen.
Medications were counted by active ingredient, with fixed combinations counted as two and oral carbonic anhydrase inhibitors counted as one.
Best-corrected visual acuity (BCVA) was converted to logMAR.
When performed per clinician judgement, endothelial cell density (ECD) was captured and measured by specular microscopy.
No reading center was employed, and measurements were verified for quality in the study's data management process.
Allograft position was assessed by gonioscopy.

Effectiveness outcomes were: mean changes in medicated IOP and number of medications from baseline to Month 24 in each cohort, the proportions of eyes with ≥ 20% IOP reduction and with IOP ≤ 18 and ≤ 15 mmHg, and composite responders achieving the same IOP thresholds without increase in medications from baseline or secondary IOP-lowering procedures.
Additional outcomes assessed were rates of secondary IOP-lowering procedures, change in visual acuity, and change in ECD.
Time to reoperation was estimated by the Kaplan-Meier method with complementary log-log confidence intervals.
Eyes without an event were censored at their last recorded study visit.

Safety outcomes were prospectively defined adverse events: clinical hypotony, choroidal effusion or folds, hyphema > 2 mm, loss of ≥ 2 lines of visual acuity at ≥ 90 days, IOP elevation ≥ 10 mmHg above baseline > 30 days after surgery, macular edema, confirmed visual field mean deviation worsening ≥ 2.5 dB, retinal complications, uveitis, and unplanned surgical reintervention, in addition to all other ocular adverse events.
text.formatted: Safety outcomes were prospectively defined adverse events: clinical hypotony, choroidal effusion or folds, hyphema > 2 mm, loss of ≥ 2 lines of visual acuity at ≥ 90 days, IOP elevation ≥ 10 mmHg above baseline > 30 days after surgery, macular edema, confirmed visual field mean deviation worsening ≥ 2.5 dB, retinal complications, uveitis, and unplanned surgical reintervention, in addition to all other ocular adverse events.

text.text: Two definitions are distinguished and reported separately throughout.
A secondary IOP-lowering procedure is any procedure performed to provide sustained IOP reduction and is the event that governs censoring for efficacy assessments.
Anterior chamber paracentesis and bleb needling or revision are not counted as censoring procedures; all other IOP-lowering procedures result in censoring at the time they are performed.
Reoperation counts incisional surgeries only, excluding laser procedures, and is the endpoint of the Kaplan-Meier analysis.

The primary analysis used a while-on-treatment strategy, excluding values recorded after a secondary procedure, so efficacy estimates describe eyes managed with the index procedure and medication without confounding from subsequent procedures.
Composite responder analyses were calculated on all eyes attending Month 24, with eyes undergoing a secondary procedure counted as non-responders.
A sensitivity analysis was performed in which eyes with a secondary IOP-lowering procedure were assigned their baseline IOP and medication count and classed as non-responders.
Continuous variables, including number of medications, are summarized as mean ± standard deviation (SD), and IOP is reported as mean with 95% confidence interval (CI).

Within-cohort changes from baseline were tested with the paired t-test, the change in the proportion of medication-free eyes with McNemar's exact test, and confidence intervals for mean changes and for mean percentage changes are t-based.
Both eyes of some patients were included, and all data were analyzed at the eye level without adjustment for inter-eye correlation [15].

text.text: Because baseline medicated IOP in Cohort 1 ranged from 9 to 32 mmHg, eyes were stratified by baseline medicated IOP and analyzed in three tiers: low (≤ 15 mmHg), moderate (16) (17) (18) (19) (20) and high (≥ 21 mmHg).

Missing data were handled by complete-case analysis without imputation.
Analyses were performed in R version (R Foundation for Statistical Computing).

text.text: A total of 176 eyes in Cohort 1 and 32 in Cohort 2 met the eligibility criteria and were included for analysis.

Before Month 24, 9 eyes in each cohort underwent a secondary IOP-lowering procedure; these eyes were excluded from the primary efficacy analyses, leaving N=167 and N=23 eyes in Cohort 1 and 2, respectively for efficacy analysis.
These eyes were retained in the sensitivity, time-to-event, and safety analyses.
Demographics and baseline characteristics are shown in Table 1.
text.formatted: Demographics and baseline characteristics are shown in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>.

text.text: Cohort 1 eyes (all phakic) had a mean age of 71.2 ± 7.5 years, 51.1% were female and 48.9% male, and mean baseline IOP was 17.9 mmHg (17.2, 18.6) on 1.4 ± 1.3 medications.
Most eyes with visual field data (54.1%) had mild disease.
Baseline IOP tiers comprised 35.8% of eyes in the low tier (≤ 15 mmHg), 40.3% moderate (16-20 mmHg), and 23.9% high (≥ 21 mmHg).
Low-tier eyes carried the heaviest medication burden (1.9 ± 1.5 medications), consistent with pressure controlled by medication.
Cohort 2 eyes had a mean age of 73.8 ± 8.5 years, 59.4% were female and 40.6% male, 96.9% were pseudophakic, and mean baseline IOP was 20.8 mmHg (18.9, 22.8) on 2.9 ± 1.2 medications.

The baseline IOP distribution in Cohort 2 was 12.5% low, 31.3% moderate, and 56.3% high; these proportions are descriptive only, and the stratified analysis was confined to Cohort 1, which was the only cohort large enough to support tier-level estimates.

In this multicenter registry, allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis lowered both IOP and medication burden on average in both cohorts.

The IOP-lowering effect was more pronounced in the standalone population (Cohort 2), where baseline pressure was much higher than in the phacocombined cohort (Cohort 1), in which eyes were mostly controlled and the therapeutic objective is often medication reduction.

When combined with phacoemulsification, the procedure lowered medicated IOP by 3.1 mmHg and medication use by 0.5 from a mean baseline of 18.0 mmHg; performed standalone, it lowered IOP by 6.4 mmHg (27.1%) and medication use by 1.2 from 20.0 mmHg in eyes managed without further surgery.
Nearly half of phaco-combined eyes and three in ten standalone eyes were controlled on no glaucoma medication at 24 months.
No eye developed clinically significant hypotony or choroidal effusion.
More eyes in the standalone cohort needed secondary incisional surgery for optimal IOP control.
The two cohorts represent distinct, clinically selected real-world populations.

At baseline, the standalone population (Cohort 2) had higher mean medicated IOP than the phaco-combined population (Cohort 1; 20.8 versus 17.9 mmHg) despite approximately twice as many glaucoma medications (2.9 versus 1.4 agents); 56.3% versus 23.9% of eyes had baseline IOP ≥21 mmHg.

These differences fit a paradigm in which intervention during cataract surgery often reduces medication burden while maintaining pressure control, whereas standalone intervention addresses the need for additional IOP lowering despite substantial medical therapy.

Similar selection patterns are reported for other MIGS procedures: in the iStent inject series of Guedes et al., standalone eyes had higher baseline IOP and medication use (17.8 mmHg on 2.60 medications versus 16.0 mmHg on 2.14) [18], and Hengerer et al. reported greater baseline pressure, medication burden, and prior glaucoma procedures in standalone eyes [19].

Standalone eyes requiring further intervention had higher baseline IOP than those remaining in the primary efficacy analysis (22.8 versus 20.0 mmHg).
The primary estimate consequently describes outcomes while eyes remained managed with the index procedure and medications, rather than outcomes across the entire original cohort.

In the failure-inclusive sensitivity analysis, these eyes were assigned their baseline IOP and medication counts, yielding a more conservative standalone reduction of 4.6 mmHg, with 50% achieving ≥20% reduction.

The findings therefore support sustained IOP and medication reductions through 24 months in eyes managed without further procedures, alongside a clinically relevant need for additional intervention in about onequarter of standalone eyes.

Comparisons with other MIGS provide context but do not establish superiority or equivalence, and the combined-surgery findings cannot distinguish the contribution of allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis from that of phacoemulsification.

The observed safety profile of allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis was broadly consistent with established canal-based MIGS, for which hyphema, transient IOP elevation, and anteriorsegment inflammation are characteristic postoperative events.

A meta-analysis of 95 studies encompassing 9,733 eyes found no increase in sight-threatening events with phaco-combined MIGS compared with phacoemulsification alone, although pooled hyphema rates varied by mechanism: 3.5% for trabecular bypass, 15.5% for non-GATT goniotomy, and 27.7% for GATT [28].

Overall ocular adverse events, serious ocular adverse events, and protocol-defined IOP elevations were numerically more frequent in standalone than phaco-combined CREST eyes (28.1% versus 18.2%, 6.2% versus 2.3%, and 9.4% versus 4.0%, respectively).
Six eyes experienced serious ocular events, including two standalone events unresolved at the analysis cutoff.

Although procedure-related event rates were low and similar between cohorts, the contribution of baseline disease burden to these differences cannot be determined from this unmatched observational analysis.
The findings therefore support a favorable observed safety profile, without establishing equivalence to other MIGS.

In the CREST specular-microscopy subset, endothelial cell density declined by 8.4% at 24 months in 34 phacocombined eyes, with no detectable change in standalone eyes.

This loss was numerically lower than the 13.1% with phaco-iStent inject and 12.3% with phacoemulsification alone in the pivotal trial, although the small, real-world CREST subset, without a reading center or protocolized specular microscopy, precludes inference of superior endothelial preservation [6].

text.text: The absence of corneal decompensation and of recorded allograft-cornea contact may partly reflect the compliant, homologous acellular scleral tissue and its placement within the supraciliary cleft, clear of the corneal endothelium.

Compared with exogenous hardware, this tissue-based construct offers a plausible rationale for reduced mechanical irritation and foreign-body response; however, neither mechanism was directly measured, and material composition cannot be separated from positioning, geometry, or surgical technique.
The results therefore support the biological rationale for allograft reinforcement without establishing superior biocompatibility or corneal and angle safety.

Optional endothelial measurements, small evaluable subsets, and nonstandardized synechiae characterization warrant longer follow-up with serial specular microscopy and anatomically defined gonioscopic grading.
The cleft was recorded as open around the allograft in 18 eyes (11.5%) at Month 24.

Because no eye had allograft-cornea contact and the allograft was optimally positioned in 89.7%, this appearance is more consistent with a cleft that remains patent beyond the allograft footprint, and therefore with continued uveoscleral flow, than with displacement of the tissue.
The converse finding of partial or total synechiae in 15 eyes may represent gradual remodeling of the cleft margins.
Both readings are descriptive because gonioscopic appearance was not graded against a predefined anatomic scale.
No secondary allograft migration was reported through 24 months.

This may reflect the compliant scleral tissue conforming to the endoscleral wall, with close tissue apposition and frictional engagement as plausible mechanisms of retention, although surface friction and fixation strength were not measured, and greater resistance to migration than metal or polymer implants has not been established.

This is the largest multicenter report of 24-month safety and effectiveness for allograftreinforced cyclodialysis, and it draws on prospectively collected data with protocol-defined adverse event categories.
Several limitations qualify these findings.

The design is observational and single-arm, so in the combined cohort the contribution of the allograft procedure cannot be separated from that of phacoemulsification; only a randomized comparison can do that.
IOP was measured on medication without washout, so these values are not comparable with pivotal trials that used washout.

The two cohorts differed substantially in baseline pressure, medication burden and disease severity, were not matched, and are therefore reported separately without a formal between-cohort test of effectiveness.

Stratification by baseline pressure was exploratory and unadjusted for multiplicity, and because tier membership is defined by the same measurement from which change is calculated, tier-level changes remain susceptible to regression to the mean.

The standalone cohort comprised 23 eyes in the primary analysis, which limits the precision of every estimate derived from it, and the 9 eyes that underwent a secondary procedure had higher baseline pressure, so the failure-inclusive estimate is the more conservative description.
Specular microscopy was optional, as real-world standard of care does not include ECD biometry for glaucoma procedures, so endothelial estimates rest on a limited subset of eyes.

Lastly, both eyes of 50 patients were included and analyzed at the eye level without adjustment for inter-eye correlation (baseline IOP r = 0.73, Month 24 r = 0.56), so confidence intervals may be modestly narrow.
Follow-up beyond 24 months is not yet available, and the durability of cleft patency over 469 longer intervals remains unknown.

Allograft-reinforced cyclodialysis, performed alone or with phacoemulsification, was associated 472 with significant reductions in medicated IOP and medication burden sustained through 2 years, 473 with an increased proportion of eyes requiring no medication and a favorable observed safety 474 profile consistent with a minimally invasive ab-interno intervention.
